Respiratory Anatomy — Part 2: neck, larynx, thorax & lungs

From where Pt 1 left off — down the neck, through the larynx, into the thoracic bellows, and out to the alveoli. The whole lower airway and the machinery that ventilates it, decoded from Dr Madden's lecture with its own figures.

Covers LO 6–15 18 plates Clinical throughout Recall checklist

How to use this guide

Each section carries a reference code like §7.1. Every figure is a Plate with a Label Key; tables summarise, prose explains. The coloured tags mark the extras:

Reasoning

§0orientation

Orientation — the airway and its bellows

Where Pt 1 left off, and the order we build the rest.

Pt 1 covered the skull, nasal cavity and sinuses — the top of the airway. This lecture (Pt 2) works downward and outward: it finishes the neck (the triangles, fascia and muscles the airway runs through), builds the larynx (the valve between throat and trachea), then the thoracic wall, diaphragm and pleura — the bellows — and finally the lungs and the alveolar surface where gas is actually exchanged.

Reasoning · airway vs bellows

Breathing needs two things: a tube for air (nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → alveoli) and a pump to move air through it (the thoracic wall, diaphragm and the pleural seal). This guide builds the tube top-down (§3–§4, §9) and the pump (§5–§8) alongside it, then joins them at gas exchange (§10). Keep asking of each structure: is it part of the pipe or part of the pump?

§1LO6 · neck

Neck — triangles & fascia

The SCM splits the neck into two working spaces, wrapped in sliding fascial sleeves.

Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) divides each side of the neck into an anterior and a posterior triangle — a standard way to organise what runs where.

The two triangles of the neck
Posterior triangleAnterior triangle
BoundariesAnterior border of trapezius (post), SCM (ant), middle 1/3 of the clavicle (inf)SCM, midline, inferior border of mandible
Key contentsCN XI (accessory), brachial plexus, subclavian vein + distal subclavian artery, external jugular, posterior belly of omohyoid, splenius capitis / levator scapulae / scalenesSupra- & infrahyoid muscles, carotid bifurcation, internal jugular, CN VII, IX, X, XI, XII, hyoid, thyroid gland & cartilage, glands & lymph nodes

§1.1Fascial layers

The neck's structures are wrapped in a superficial fascia (deep to the dermis, blending with platysma; carries superficial veins like the external jugular, lymph nodes, fat) and four deep fascial layers:

  • Investing layer — the most superficial deep layer; surrounds all neck structures and splits to enclose trapezius and SCM.
  • Pretracheal layer — a muscular part (encloses the infrahyoid muscles) + a visceral part (encloses thyroid, trachea and oesophagus).
  • Prevertebral layer — wraps the vertebral column, scalenes, levator scapulae and longus capitis, and the sympathetic trunk.
  • Carotid sheath — a tube carrying the vagus nerve (CN X), internal jugular vein and common carotid artery.

Plate 1.1 shows the layers in cross-section.

Label Key
Investing layer
Surrounds all; splits around trapezius & SCM.
Pretracheal / prevertebral
Enclose the viscera (thyroid/trachea/oesophagus) / the vertebral column & sympathetic trunk.
Carotid sheath
Vagus (CN X), internal jugular vein, common carotid artery.
Reasoning · why wrap the neck in sleeves

The fascial layers do two jobs. They let structures glide past each other — you swallow, turn your head and phonate while the trachea, oesophagus and vessels slide independently. And they create compartments that contain and channel: the carotid sheath is a protected conduit, and the pretracheal/prevertebral planes both guide and limit how infection or blood spreads. Learn the planes and you can predict where a neck abscess will track.

Clinical / real-world · the exposed posterior triangle

The accessory nerve (CN XI) runs superficially across the posterior triangle, so it's easily injured in surgery/biopsy there → a drooping shoulder (trapezius palsy). And the brachial plexus + subclavian vessels emerging between the scalenes here are what can be compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome.

§2LO6 · neck

Neck muscles

Elevators and depressors of the hyoid — the larynx's moving anchor.

The hyoid bone is slung between two muscle groups that raise and lower it (and the larynx with it) — essential for swallowing and phonation.

Hyoid muscles
GroupMusclesAction
SuprahyoidDigastric (anterior + posterior belly), mylohyoid, stylohyoidElevate the hyoid/larynx
Infrahyoid ("strap")Sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoidDepress the hyoid/larynx

Plate 2.1 shows the suprahyoid muscles; Plate 2.2 the infrahyoid ("strap") muscles.

Label Key
Digastric (ant + post belly), mylohyoid, stylohyoid
Elevate the hyoid/larynx in swallowing.
Label Key
Sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid
Depress the hyoid/larynx; named origin-to-insertion.

The posterior triangle also floors out with muscles you'll meet again in respiration: splenius capitis, levator scapulae, middle & anterior scalene, and the inferior belly of omohyoid.

Reasoning · why elevate the larynx to swallow

During swallowing the suprahyoids haul the larynx up and forward under the tongue base, which tips the epiglottis down over the airway and seals it — so food goes to the oesophagus, not the trachea. The infrahyoids then reset it. Read the group name (supra/infra) and you know the direction of pull. The scalenes here double as accessory muscles of respiration (§7) — hold that thought.

Memory hook · the strap muscles

The four infrahyoids are named origin-to-insertion: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid (omo = shoulder/scapula). Read the name → know both ends.

§3LO7 · larynx

Larynx — cartilages & vocal cords

A cartilage box that guards the airway and makes the voice.

The larynx is a framework of cartilages (some named for their shape) linked by ligaments and moved by small muscles.

Laryngeal cartilages
CartilageShape / note
Thyroid"Shield" — the largest; forms the laryngeal prominence
Cricoid"Ring" — the only complete ring in the airway
Arytenoid"Funnel" — paired; anchor the vocal cords
Corniculate"Horn" — paired; sit on the arytenoids
EpiglottisLeaf-shaped flap that covers the airway in swallowing

Inside, two pairs of folds: the false vocal cords (vestibular folds) above and the true vocal cords (vocal folds) below. Key ligaments: the cricothyroid and hyo-thyroid ligaments.

Plate 3.1 shows the cartilages from several views; Plate 3.2 the interior with the vocal cords, epiglottis and ligaments.

Label Key
Thyroid (shield) · cricoid (ring)
Cricoid is the only complete ring.
Arytenoid (funnel) · corniculate (horn)
Paired; anchor/act on the vocal cords.
Label Key
False (vestibular) vs true (vocal) folds
Two pairs of folds; the true folds phonate.
Epiglottis; cricothyroid & hyo-thyroid ligaments
Airway cover; key connecting ligaments.
Clinical / real-world · why the cricoid ring matters

Because the cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring, it's the one level that can't collapse — which is why cricoid pressure is applied during intubation (to occlude the oesophagus behind it) and why the cricothyroid membrane, just above it, is the site for an emergency surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy) when the upper airway is blocked.

§4LO7–8 · larynx

Larynx — muscles, divisions & neurovasculature

The muscles that tune the cords, the three floors, and the nerve that risks the voice.

§4.1Intrinsic muscles

The intrinsic muscles are named from where they start to where they end: cricothyroid, posterior cricoarytenoid, lateral cricoarytenoid, transverse & oblique arytenoids, and thyroarytenoid. Together they open, close and tense the vocal cords.

Reasoning · the one muscle that opens the airway

Among all these, the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only ABDUCTOR — the only muscle that opens the glottis. Everything else adducts/tenses. That makes it critical: lose it on both sides (bilateral nerve injury) and the cords sit closed → airway obstruction. "Posterior cricoarytenoid = Pulls cords aPart."

§4.2Divisions & histology

The three divisions of the larynx
DivisionFunctionEpithelium
SupraglottisProtect the airwayRespiratory (pseudostratified ciliated columnar)
Glottis (vocal folds)PhonationStratified squamous (resists mechanical stress)
SubglottisSupport the cords; entrance to the tracheaRespiratory (pseudostratified ciliated columnar)

Plate 4.1 shows the three divisions.

Label Key
Supraglottis / glottis / subglottis
Protect / phonate / support the cords & enter the trachea.
Epithelium
Glottis = stratified squamous; elsewhere = respiratory epithelium.
Reasoning · why the glottis has different skin

The vocal folds slam together and vibrate hundreds of times a second, so the glottis is lined with tough stratified squamous epithelium (like skin) that resists mechanical stress — while the rest of the larynx keeps the respiratory epithelium that cleans and humidifies air. Epithelium follows function: abuse → squamous; airflow → ciliated.

§4.3Nerve & blood supply

The vagus (CN X) supplies the larynx through two branches:

  • Superior laryngeal nerve — internal branch = sensation to the supraglottic mucosa; external branch = motor to cricothyroid only.
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve (becomes the inferior laryngeal) — motor to all other intrinsic muscles and sensation below the cords.

Arteries mirror the nerves: the superior laryngeal artery (external carotid → superior thyroid) and the inferior laryngeal artery (subclavian → thyrocervical → inferior thyroid); the veins drain the same territories to the internal jugular and brachiocephalic.

Clinical / real-world · the recurrent laryngeal nerve & a hoarse voice

The recurrent laryngeal nerve takes a long detour — and the left one loops under the arch of the aorta in the chest, so it's uniquely vulnerable to thoracic disease (aortic aneurysm, a lung/mediastinal tumour) as well as thyroid surgery. Damage it and you lose every intrinsic muscle except cricothyroid → a hoarse voice (or, if bilateral, a threatened airway). A new hoarseness can be the first sign of chest pathology.

§5LO9 · thorax

Thoracic cavity, apertures & wall

The box the lungs live in — its rooms, its doorways, and its moving walls.

The thoracic cavity has three compartments: a central mediastinum (heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus) flanked by two pulmonary (pleural) cavities (the lungs, bronchial tree and pleura).

Plate 5.1 shows the cavity in cross-section — mediastinum centrally, pleural cavities either side.

Label Key
Mediastinum (centre)
Heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus.
Pulmonary/pleural cavities (L & R)
Lungs, bronchial tree and pleura.

§5.1The apertures

The box is open top and bottom. The superior thoracic aperture (inlet) lets the trachea, oesophagus and great vessels pass to the neck. The inferior thoracic aperture (outlet) — bounded by the xiphoid/costal margin (ant), 10th rib (lat) and 12th rib/T12 (post) — is sealed by the diaphragm, with only the aorta, IVC and oesophagus passing through.

§5.2The thoracic wall & ribs

Rib classification
TypeRibsAttachment
True1–7Own costal cartilage directly to the sternum
False8–10Cartilage joins the rib above (shared) — not the sternum directly
Floating11–12No anterior attachment

A typical rib has a head, neck, tubercle and body/shaft, articulating with the vertebrae at the costovertebral (body) and costotransverse (tubercle) joints.

Reasoning · why ribs are jointed, not fused

The rib cage has to be rigid enough to protect the heart and lungs yet mobile enough to breathe. The paired costovertebral/costotransverse joints set a fixed axis so each rib swings up and out ("bucket handle / pump handle") to enlarge the cavity — the mechanical basis of the inhalation in §7. Floating ribs stay free to allow the lower cage to flare.

§6LO10 · diaphragm

The diaphragm

The main muscle of breathing — a domed floor with three doorways and one nerve.

The diaphragm seals the thoracic outlet. Its parts: a central tendon, a muscular part (sternal + costal fibres), the crura (left & right, anchoring to the lumbar spine), and the median arcuate ligament.

The three hiatuses
HiatusLevelPasses through
CavalT8 — in the central tendonIVC (+ right phrenic nerve)
OesophagealT10 — in the muscular cruraOesophagus (+ vagal trunks)
AorticT12 — behind the diaphragmAorta (+ thoracic duct, azygos)

Plate 6.1 shows the diaphragm from below (central tendon, crura, hiatuses); Plate 6.2 the phrenic neurovasculature.

Label Key
Central tendon & muscular part
Non-contractile tendon centrally; sternal + costal muscle.
Crura & hiatuses
Left/right crura; caval (T8), oesophageal (T10), aortic (T12).
Label Key
Phrenic nerve (C3–5)
Motor + sensory to the diaphragm; palsy raises a hemidiaphragm.
Phrenic vessels
Superior/inferior phrenic arteries supplying the diaphragm.
Reasoning · why each doorway is where it is

The openings are placed to exploit the muscle's mechanics. The IVC passes through the non-contractile central tendon, so diaphragm contraction doesn't pinch the vein shut — venous return continues (and is even helped) during inspiration. The oesophagus passes through the muscular crura, so contraction squeezes it — a physiological anti-reflux sphincter. Structure placed for function.

Clinical / real-world · phrenic nerve & referred pain

The diaphragm's motor and sensory nerve is the phrenic (C3, 4, 5). Two consequences: (1) a phrenic palsy paralyses that hemidiaphragm, so it sits high and moves paradoxically — you can read which side is affected from the raised lobe. (2) Because C3–5 also supplies the skin over the shoulder, diaphragm irritation (blood, infection, gallbladder) is felt as referred pain in the shoulder tip.

Memory hook · phrenic roots & hiatus levels

"C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive." Hiatus levels step by 2s: T8 caVa (IVC), T10 oesophagus (10 letters), T12 aorta.

§7LO11 · mechanics

Muscles of respiration

Quiet breathing is nearly free; forced breathing calls in reserves.

Beyond the diaphragm, the intercostals (external, internal, innermost), plus subcostal and transversus thoracis, move the ribs; the accessory muscles (scalenes and others in the neck/upper thorax) join in when demand rises.

The mechanics of a breath
PhaseWhat moves
Quiet inhalationDiaphragm ↑ vertical dimension; external intercostals elevate ribs → ↑ horizontal dimension
Quiet exhalationPassive recoil (no muscle work)
Forced inhalationAccessory muscles (neck/upper thorax) elevate the ribcage
Forced exhalationInternal intercostals depress the ribs; abdominals raise intra-abdominal pressure → push the diaphragm up

Plate 7.1 shows the thoracic-wall muscles; Plate 7.2 the mechanics of quiet inhalation vs exhalation.

Label Key
External / internal / innermost intercostals
Elevate (inspire) / depress (forced expire) the ribs.
Subcostal · transversus thoracis · scalenes
Additional + accessory respiratory muscles.
Label Key
Quiet inhalation
Diaphragm ↑ vertical; external intercostals ↑ horizontal.
Quiet exhalation
Passive elastic recoil — no muscle work.
Reasoning · why quiet exhalation is "free"

Inhalation is active — muscles enlarge the cavity, dropping the pressure so air flows in. Quiet exhalation is passive: the stretched lungs and chest wall simply recoil like a released spring, needing no muscle. You only recruit the internal intercostals and abdominals when you need to push air out fast (exercise, coughing) — which is why breathing at rest costs so little energy.

§7.1The intercostal neurovascular bundle

In the costal groove on the underside of each rib runs the neurovascular bundle in the order Vein–Artery–Nerve (VAN), superior to inferior, with a collateral supply below.

Plate 7.3 shows the bundle and the safe drain site.

Label Key
VAN in the costal groove
Vein–Artery–Nerve, superior→inferior, under the rib.
Safe drain site
Mid/lower space, above the rib below, to avoid the bundle.
Clinical / real-world · where to put a chest drain

Because the VAN bundle hugs the underside of each rib, you insert a needle or chest drain in the mid/lower intercostal space, just ABOVE the rib below — that skims the space where only the smaller collateral vessels run and avoids the main bundle tucked under the rib above. Geometry dictates technique.

§8LO12 · pleura

The pleura

Two slippery sheets and the film of fluid that couples lung to wall.

Each lung is wrapped in a double serous membrane: the visceral pleura (on the lung surface) is continuous at the hilum with the parietal pleura (lining the thoracic wall) — the parietal pleura has four regions (cervical, costal, mediastinal, diaphragmatic). Between them the pleural space holds a thin film of serous fluid for frictionless movement, and dips into two recesses the lung doesn't fully fill.

Plate 8.1 shows the pleural regions, space and recesses.

Label Key
Visceral vs parietal
Lung surface vs thoracic wall; 4 parietal regions.
Pleural space & recesses
Serous fluid for frictionless movement; recesses the lung doesn't fill.
Reasoning · why the pleura makes the lung follow the wall

The fluid film does what water between two glass slides does — it lets them slide freely but not pull apart. So when the thoracic wall and diaphragm expand (§7), the parietal pleura goes with them and drags the visceral pleura — and the lung — outward, dropping the pressure and pulling air in. Break the seal (air in the space = pneumothorax) and the lung recoils and collapses, because nothing is holding it out any more.

Clinical / real-world · why lung cancer can be painless

Parietal pleura is supplied by somatic nerves (intercostal + phrenic), so it is exquisitely pain-sensitive and well-localised — inflame it and you get sharp pleuritic pain. Visceral pleura has only autonomic supply (pulmonary plexus) and is insensitive to pain — which is why a tumour deep in the lung can grow silently until it reaches the parietal pleura or chest wall. The costodiaphragmatic recess is also the lowest point where fluid (an effusion) pools and where it's tapped.

§9LO13 · lungs

Bronchial tree & lungs

A branching pipe that trades cartilage for muscle, feeding two asymmetric lungs.

§9.1The bronchial tree

Air passes through a conducting zone (no alveoli, no gas exchange — just plumbing) before reaching the respiratory zone. The branches go primary (main) → secondary (lobar) → tertiary (segmental) bronchi, and the wall changes as you descend: cartilage decreases, smooth muscle increases; once there's no cartilage, it's a bronchiole.

Plate 9.1 shows the conducting vs respiratory zones and the bronchial levels.

Label Key
Conducting vs respiratory zone
No gas exchange (plumbing) vs where exchange happens.
Primary → secondary → tertiary
↓ cartilage, ↑ smooth muscle; no cartilage = bronchiole.
Reasoning · cartilage rings → muscle sleeves

Big airways need to stay propped open against pressure swings, so they're ringed with cartilage. Small airways instead need adjustable calibre to distribute airflow, so they trade cartilage for smooth muscle. That's why the small, cartilage-free bronchioles are exactly where bronchoconstriction happens — the anatomical basis of asthma and why bronchodilators target smooth muscle.

§9.2The lungs — left vs right

Comparing the lungs
Left lungRight lung
Lobes / fissures2 lobes, oblique fissure3 lobes, oblique + horizontal fissures
ImpressionsCardiac notch + aortic impressionAzygos vein impression
Both: apex (from the superior lobe), a diaphragmatic surface, anterior/posterior/inferior borders, and a hilum transmitting the bronchi and vessels.

Plate 9.2 labels the lobes, fissures, borders, surfaces, hilum and impressions.

Label Key
Left (2 lobes, cardiac notch) vs right (3 lobes)
Oblique fissure both; horizontal fissure right only.
Hilum, borders, surfaces, impressions
Bronchi/vessels enter at the hilum; mediastinal structures impress the surface.
Reasoning · why the two lungs differ

The heart sits left of midline, so the left lung gives up room — two lobes and a scooped cardiac notch. The right keeps three lobes. This has a hidden clinical payoff: the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, so an inhaled foreign body (or aspiration) preferentially goes right. Asymmetry you can see explains a pattern you'll diagnose.

§10LO14 · flow & exchange

Blood flow, innervation & gas exchange

Two blood supplies, one autonomic dial, and the paper-thin barrier where it all happens.

The lung has a dual blood supply, doing two different jobs:

  • Bronchial circulation — nutritive. Bronchial arteries from the thoracic aorta feed the lung tissue itself (oxygenated systemic blood).
  • Pulmonary circulation — functional. The right ventricle → pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the alveoli; the pulmonary veins → left atrium return oxygenated blood. (The one place arteries carry deoxygenated blood and veins carry oxygenated.)

Innervation is via the pulmonary plexus: PNS = vagus, SNS = sympathetic trunk. Sympathetic activity dilates the bronchioles (opening the airway for exertion).

Plate 10.1 shows the dual supply and innervation.

Label Key
Bronchial a. (nutritive)
From the thoracic aorta — feeds lung tissue.
Pulmonary a./v. (functional)
RV → pulmonary a. (deoxygenated) → lungs → pulmonary v. (oxygenated) → LA.

§10.1The alveolus & respiratory membrane

At the end of the tree, gas is exchanged across a wall built from a few cell types:

  • Type I pneumocytes — thin, flat cells that do the gas exchange.
  • Type II pneumocytes — make surfactant.
  • Endothelial cells (capillary) and alveolar macrophages (defence).

The respiratory membrane — the actual barrier O₂ and CO₂ cross — is just Type I pneumocyte + fused basement membrane + capillary endothelial cell.

Plate 10.2 shows the alveolar cells and the respiratory membrane.

Label Key
Type I / II pneumocytes
Type I = gas exchange; Type II = surfactant.
Respiratory membrane
Type I pneumocyte + basement membrane + endothelial cell.
Reasoning · thin for gas, and why surfactant matters

Diffusion is fastest across the thinnest, largest surface — so the respiratory membrane is squeezed to three flat layers over a huge alveolar area. But thin, wet alveoli want to collapse from surface tension, so Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant to lower that tension and keep them open. This is why premature babies (too little surfactant) develop respiratory distress syndrome — the anatomy of the alveolus predicts the disease.

§11LO15 · surface

Surface anatomy

Projecting the fissures and borders onto the living chest.

Knowing where the lobes and pleura project lets you listen to the right lobe and tap fluid safely.

Fissure projections
FissureCourse
Right obliqueT4 vertebra → 6/7 intercostal space, along the inferior border of the 6th rib
Right horizontalT4 vertebra → 5/6 intercostal space → medial 4th rib
Left obliqueT4 vertebra → 6/7 intercostal space → inferior border of the 6th rib

Surface landmarks around the chest include the costal margin, serratus anterior, external oblique, floor of the axilla, latissimus dorsi and pectoralis major. Plate 11.1 maps them.

Label Key
Fissure projections
Oblique → 6th rib; right horizontal → 4th rib.
Landmarks
Costal margin, serratus anterior, axilla, lat dorsi, pec major.
Clinical / real-world · lung vs pleura edges

The pleura extends lower than the lung (the lung's inferior border sits a couple of ribs above the pleural reflection, leaving the costodiaphragmatic recess, §8). That gap is why a needle placed too low can enter pleura without hitting lung — useful for draining an effusion, and a trap if you misjudge the level. Projecting the fissures also tells you which lobe you're auscultating at each spot on the chest.

R Recall checklist — Respiratory Pt 2
  • Neck triangles — posterior (trapezius/SCM/clavicle; CN XI, brachial plexus, subclavian vessels) vs anterior (carotid bifurcation, IJV, CN VII/IX/X/XI/XII, thyroid).
  • Cervical fascia — investing, pretracheal (muscular + visceral), prevertebral (+ sympathetic trunk), carotid sheath (CN X, IJV, common carotid).
  • Neck muscles — suprahyoid (elevate) vs infrahyoid straps (depress); posterior triangle = splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenes, omohyoid.
  • Larynx — cartilages (thyroid/cricoid[only ring]/arytenoid/corniculate/epiglottis); false vs true cords; divisions (supraglottis/glottis[squamous]/subglottis); posterior cricoarytenoid = only abductor; CN X (superior laryngeal + recurrent laryngeal).
  • Thorax — cavity (mediastinum + 2 pleural cavities); apertures (inlet/outlet); ribs true(1–7)/false(8–10)/floating(11–12); costovertebral + costotransverse joints.
  • Diaphragm — central tendon, crura, median arcuate ligament; hiatuses caval T8/oesophageal T10/aortic T12; phrenic C3–5; referred shoulder pain.
  • Respiration — quiet: diaphragm + external intercostals (in), passive recoil (out); forced: accessory (in), internal intercostals + abdominals (out). Intercostal VAN in costal groove → drain above the rib.
  • Pleura — visceral vs parietal (4 regions), pleural space + serous fluid, recesses; parietal = somatic (pain), visceral = autonomic (no pain).
  • Bronchial tree/lungs — conducting vs respiratory zone; primary/secondary/tertiary; ↓cartilage ↑smooth muscle → bronchiole; left 2 lobes + cardiac notch, right 3 lobes; right main bronchus → aspiration.
  • Flow & exchange — bronchial (nutritive) vs pulmonary (functional, RV→PA deoxygenated→lungs→PV→LA); pulmonary plexus (vagus/sympathetic); Type I (exchange), Type II (surfactant); respiratory membrane = Type I + basement membrane + endothelium.
  • Surface — oblique fissure T4→6th rib; right horizontal → 4th rib; pleura projects below the lung (recess for tapping).
